column4: The section joins flood foam, measured valley flow, and useful metal scum in one image: the ayah says the valleys flow بِقَدَرِهَا, then زَبَدٌ goes while what benefits people remains. It gives the section's exact contrast between passing residue and enduring benefit.

The section's pasture becomes floating dry growth; here rain enters streams in the earth and the crop yellows before Allah makes it حُطَامًا. This repeats the whole growth-to-debris movement beside the water source.

The section reads غُثَاء as dried vegetation floating on a flood; this ayah makes rain-grown vegetation هَشِيمًا scattered by winds. Its own context supplies a close image of provision's brief green stage ending in dispersed plant matter.

The section's green pasture ends as غُثَاء; this ayah likewise moves from rain-grown plants to yellowing and حُطَامًا, then applies that cycle to worldly life. It directly joins the section's vegetation image to its claim that the Hereafter is more abiding.

The section's pasture turns to debris; here rain makes the earth's growth lush, then it is harvested as though it had not flourished the day before. The abrupt loss sharpens the difference between a season's display and what remains.

The section's rock hollows gather cloud water and 13:17 measures valley flow; here water is sent down بِقَدَرٍ, settled in the earth, and can be taken away. It makes both measured storage and its limit explicit.

The section's pasture may become floating waste; this ayah says God could make the crop حُطَامًا after people sow it. The possibility of losing the harvest makes the useful growth in the section contingent rather than permanent.

The source section identifies غُثَاء as both flood-borne plants and a proverb for what disappears without value; this ayah says a punished people were made غُثَاءً. The word transfers the image of scattered refuse to a vanished community.

The section distinguishes useful water from what a torrent carries off; this ayah's rain strikes a thinly covered rock and leaves it bare, as a picture of deeds that yield nothing. It makes the loss of apparent benefit concrete.

The section's hollows and wells hold water until it appears clear; this garden owner's water may instead become غَوْرًا, beyond his reach. That is the image's direct boundary: stored water can disappear below the ground.

The section follows water gathered in rock hollows and wells; this ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it became غَوْرًا. It turns the section's available, retained water into a stated dependence on God.

The section's dictionary form خَلِيقَة names a rock hollow collecting rain; here water bursts from a struck rock into twelve springs, and each group عَلِمَ its drinking place. The ayah gives both a rock-water scene and the source section's علم family beside an assigned water source.

The section's خَلِيقَة is a hollow in rock where water gathers; here twelve springs gush from the rock and each group عَلِمَ its drinking place. The springs emerge rather than collect, but the ayah supplies a close rock-and-water counterpart and the named علم family.

The section's dictionary entry describes water collected in hollows in rock; this ayah says some stones split and water comes out. The direction differs, but it makes the rock itself a source or vessel for water.

The section describes a flood and what its current carries away; after Noah's flood, the earth is told to swallow its water and the sky to stop. This is the flood's recession, a counterpart to the section's gathering and flow.

The section names hollows filled by a torrent; this ayah names the flood of the dam, which replaces Sheba's fruitful gardens with scant, bitter growth. It shows a flood removing the landscape's useful abundance.

This precedes 34:16's flood: it describes Sheba's two gardens and tells them to eat their Lord's provision. That prior fertility makes the next ayah's flood-driven loss a specific reversal of useful growth.

After 13:17's foam-and-water parable, this ayah distinguishes those who answer their Lord from those who refuse and face a bad return. It supplies the response-side application of the section's reminder that benefits when it takes hold.
The section explicitly links 13:17's بِقَدَرِهَا to the root of 87:3; here water is sent بِقَدَرٍ and revives a dead land. It joins measured rain to growth rather than to flood residue.

The section's well is cleaned until its water appears clear; this ayah calls rainwater طَهُورًا. It gives a Quranic image of water as purifying, while the section's dictionary sense focuses on clearing a well.
The section's gathered water supports what benefits; this ayah says rain revives a dead land and gives drink to people and livestock. It shows the useful yield of water from the sky.

The section's ج ه ر dictionary entry describes clearing mud until well water emerges; this ayah sends down water to purify people. The cleansing differs in object, but makes water's removal of impurity an explicit Quranic function.

The section sets flood-borne pasture against water held in hollows; this ayah says rain provides drink and vegetation where livestock graze. It supplies the useful, living side of the same water-and-pasture scene.
The section connects cloud water with pasture and benefit; this ayah says water grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and fruit. It names the produce that makes water beneficial.
The section traces useful water to clouds and valleys; this ayah says God pours water abundantly as the beginning of the food sequence in 80:25–32. It gives the rain that makes the land productive.
The section's rain gathers in rock hollows and feeds pasture; this ayah says the earth is split open in the same food sequence. It supplies the earth's opening for growth.
The section's water sustains vegetation before it dries into refuse; this ayah names grain among the growth produced after rain and split earth. It marks the useful crop stage.
The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah adds grapes and foddering greens to the food sequence begun by rain. These are concrete yields of the water that the section follows.
The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah names olives and palms among the crops in the rain-fed sequence. It makes the growth's material benefit specific.
The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah adds dense gardens to the same sequence of crops. The gardens are the productive landscape before the section's image turns to debris.
The section follows water into useful plant growth; this ayah names fruit and أَبًّا, fodder, among the outputs of rain and split earth. The latter is especially close to pasture for grazing.
At the end of the food sequence begun with water in 80:25, this ayah calls the produce provision for people and livestock. It makes explicit the benefit of the growth the section follows.
The section's root note describes abundant water as water gathered; this ayah promises rain مِّدْرَارًا. It gives an image of abundance from the sky that fills the section's water side.
This follows 71:11's abundant rain and names gardens and rivers among God's provisions. It completes the rain-to-stored-water-to-useful-growth relation developed in the section.
The section traces cloud water into valleys and pasture; this ayah drives heavy clouds to a dead land, sends rain, and brings out fruits. Its context makes rain's productive result a sign of mercy.

This follows 7:57's rain: good land yields its plants by its Lord's permission, while bad land yields little. It gives a concrete image of different receptivity to what is provided, like the section's beneficial reminder.

The section's ج ه ر dictionary form describes cleaning a well until water appears; this ayah contrasts hidden speech with speech declared جَهَرَ. The sense is different, but the same named root frames what is concealed and what becomes manifest.

The section's 13:17 passage describes metal melted for useful objects and uses مَا يَنفَعُ النَّاسَ for what remains; this ayah names iron and its مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ. It connects the section's metal image to metal's concrete benefit.

The section mentions foam produced when metal is melted for useful things; this ayah heats iron and pours molten copper into a barrier. It is a secondary metalworking parallel, though it says nothing about foam.

The section's proverb makes غُثَاء what goes away without value; this ayah compares the deeds of disbelievers to ashes blown by a storm wind. Both images make apparent effort unable to remain or yield.
The section says غُثَاء can stand for what vanishes and is not counted; this ayah turns deeds into scattered dust. It gives a second Quranic image for value that leaves no durable remainder.

The section's cleaned-well sense is water emerging after mud is removed, and 13:17 separates foam from what benefits; this ayah says truth comes and falsehood vanishes. It gives the same clear separation in moral terms.

The section's foam is discarded while the beneficial remains; this ayah says truth is cast against falsehood until falsehood vanishes. It sharpens the image's separation into a truth-and-falsehood boundary.

After 18:45's rain-grown plants are scattered by wind, this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment and says abiding good deeds are better. It makes the section's passing pasture and lasting benefit explicit in the next ayah.

The section calls the Hereafter better and more abiding than the lower life; this ayah says not to covet worldly adornment because the Lord's provision is better and more enduring. It restates the section's measure of what lasts.

The section contrasts fading debris with the Hereafter, خير and أبقى; this ayah calls worldly life enjoyment and adornment, then says what is with God is better and more lasting. It states the same value boundary.

The section says the Hereafter is better and more abiding; this ayah names worldly provision as enjoyment and what is with God as better and more enduring. It turns the image's passing-versus-staying distinction into a judgment about provision.

The section defines ب ق ي as remaining in one's first state and opposes it to perishing; this ayah says what you have runs out while what is with God remains. It gives the exact passing-and-remaining distinction behind the image.
The section connects benefit to good and names the Hereafter as more abiding; this ayah says enduring good deeds are better in reward and return. It identifies what can remain as a useful deed.
The section contrasts fleeting surface waste with what remains; this ayah says everyone on earth is perishing. It states the boundary of created permanence that the section's image implies.
The section defines abiding as the opposite of perishing; this ayah says the face of the Lord remains. It gives the enduring side of the boundary stated in 55:26.

The section's account of what vanishes and what abides meets this ayah's claim that everything perishes except God's face. It gives the sharpest general boundary between passing creation and what remains.

The section's reminder is valuable if it benefits and its water image rests on growth; this ayah likens a good word to a good tree with a firm root and high branches. It makes the word's benefit look rooted and growing.

This continues 14:24's good-tree comparison: the tree yields fruit continually by its Lord's permission, and God gives the comparison so people may remember. It joins lasting yield to a reminder that takes root.
The section contrasts useful water with waste that leaves; this ayah likens a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability. It supplies the opposite of the good, rooted yield.
The section says the Hereafter is more abiding; this ayah says God makes believers firm in worldly life and the Hereafter. It extends the tree's stability into the two lives named by the section.

The section links rainwater and pasture; this ayah says God made the earth a cradle, sent rain from the sky, and brought out varied plants. It gives the land-and-water setting in which pasture becomes provision.

This follows the rain-grown plants in 20:53 and tells people to eat and graze their livestock. It makes explicit the useful yield of vegetation, the stage before the section's pasture turns to refuse.
